Formal theoretical analysis (Section A.5) providing rigorous justification that random FPE preserves clause coverage while reducing collisions by ~α^-(2k-1), with clear probabilistic arguments
Surprising robustness finding: random splitting nearly matches clause-aligned splitting, demonstrating that reduced parameter collisions rather than precise feature assignment drives improvements

Limited scope of real-world experiments: only small networks (≤16 hidden dims), uses fixed CLIP embeddings rather than end-to-end learning, lacks comparison with other parameter-efficient methods (LoRA, adapters, magnitude pruning, sparse training)

Ad-hoc methodological choices: re-sparsification via magnitude pruning lacks justification, alternating expansion strategy for deeper networks appears arbitrary, Gram clustering approach underdeveloped for real data

Statistical concerns: several improvements are marginal with overlapping error bars; more rigorous significance testing needed (e.g., paired t-tests); error margins in Table A4 suggest noise in some measurements

Scalability questions: heavily underparameterized networks designed to emphasize superposition; unclear how this scales to overparameterized models where superposition is less pronounced; largest experiments (ImageNet-1k) show <6% improvements for wider networks

Missing key comparisons: no comparison with magnitude pruning, structured sparsity, dynamic sparse training (beyond brief RigL mention), or other parameter-efficient methods at fixed parameter budgets; no width scaling comparisons at fixed compute

Incremental novelty: width vs. parameters explored in prior work (Golubeva et al., 2020); neuron splitting relates to known growth mechanisms (Net2Net); primary novelty is post-training application to superposition, which is modest

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical framework grounding FPE in superposition hypothesis and interpretability; solid probability-based analysis showing random FPE maintains clause coverage with high probability while reducing collisions by α^(-(2k-1))

Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning synthetic Boolean DNF tasks, vision classification at multiple scales (FashionMNIST, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k), deeper architectures (5-9 layers), and advanced sparsity patterns (2:4 structured)
Interesting empirical finding that random neuron splitting performs nearly as well as clause-aligned splitting on real tasks, suggesting architectural partitioning alone drives benefits
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Gram matrices, weight matrices) and thorough algorithmic/hyperparameter documentation enabling reproducibility

Efficiency claims are unvalidated: paper asserts FPE suits modern accelerators where memory movement dominates, but provides no wall-clock inference time, memory bandwidth, or actual hardware benchmark measurements

Real-world improvements are modest and diminish rapidly with model capacity: 2-15% on vision tasks (Fig 5), collapsing to 0.1-1% at realistic widths (Table A4: 0.1% RI for ImageNet-1k at hidden=16); benefits concentrated in narrow network regime not relevant to modern ML

Missing critical baselines and comparisons: no end-to-end training of wider networks with fixed parameters, no knowledge distillation comparison, no analysis of simple parameter addition without sparsification; pre-training confound in Section 3.4 (early splitting > late) suggests initialization effects dominate

Overclaimed practical impact: abstract claims 'interpretability-grounded mechanism' for modern accelerators despite mechanism failing on real data and efficiency benefits never being measured
